samples.summary: The anti-injection nonce is not secret from the very attacker it targets — it is handed to the browser via argv and printed to stderr
samples.evidence: The whole defence added here rests on `state` (login.ts:40) being unguessable by "another local process" (comment login.ts:33-39, docs/design/cli.md, rest-api.md risk table). But the nonce is embedded in `oauthUrl` (login.ts:44-46), which is (a) printed with `console.error` (login.ts:47) and (b) passed to `open(oauthUrl)` (login.ts:52), which spawns the browser/xdg-open with the full URL as a command-line argument. On Linux/macOS with default settings any local process — including one running as a different unprivileged user — can read that argv (`/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, `ps auxww`). Attack: local attacker polls `ps` during `wafflebase login`, reads `cliState=<nonce>` and `port=<port>`, then starts their own flow `GET /auth/github?mode=cli&port=<victim port>&cliState=<stolen nonce>` authenticating as the ATTACKER's GitHub account. The backend mints a code for the attacker's user and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<victim port>/callback?code=…&state=<stolen nonce>` (auth.controller.ts:130-135); `stateMatches` (login.ts:210) passes, the victim's CLI exchanges the attacker's code and saves the attacker's tokens as the session — the exact code-injection/session-fixation this change claims to close. A value-echo nonce cannot fix this because the value the CLI expects is the value it leaks; the standard fix is PKCE (CLI sends `code_challenge` in the URL, keeps the verifier in-process, and `POST /auth/cli/exchange` requires the verifier so a code minted for another challenge cannot be redeemed).

samples.summary: `cliState` is optional and a malformed one is silently dropped, so the backend still issues nonce-less CLI redirects — the loopback binding is opt-in, not enforced
samples.evidence: In the guard, a `cliState` that is absent, an array/object, or fails `CLI_STATE_PATTERN` becomes `undefined` (github-auth.guard.ts:31-34) and the flow is created anyway; the callback then emits `nonce = ''` (auth.controller.ts:130-132) and redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=…` with no `state` at all. Anyone can therefore start a CLI flow aimed at an arbitrary loopback port with no binding whatsoever — e.g. a page the victim visits can navigate to `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<guessed port>`. Today the new CLI rejects that (login.ts:210), so the exploit lands only against a CLI that has not been upgraded, or against any other consumer of this documented endpoint; but the server-side half of the mitigation is advisory. The server owns the redirect and should refuse `mode=cli` without a well-formed `cliState` (400) instead of silently downgrading to the pre-fix behaviour, so a bypass cannot be reintroduced from the client side.

samples.summary: `seg()` no longer rejects the empty segment, so a caller-controlled empty identifier now silently produces `//` or a trailing `/` in a credentialed URL
samples.evidence: The empty check was removed from `seg()` (url.ts:39-49), so `apiKeysUrl(cfg, '')` yields `…/api-keys/` and `apiV1Base` with an unset workspace yields `…/workspaces//documents/…`. Express runs with `strict routing` off (no `set('strict routing')` anywhere in packages/backend/src/main.ts), so `…/api-keys/` matches the *collection* route rather than `@Delete(':id')` (api-key.controller.ts:54) — i.e. an empty id no longer names the object the command names, it names its container, while still carrying the API key / Bearer token. I traced every collection-level handler under packages/backend/src/api/v1 and api-key.controller.ts and found no destructive (`@Delete()`/`@Put()`) collection route that an empty trailing segment currently reaches, so I could not complete an exploit chain — hence medium confidence and minor severity. The concern is the lost invariant: `seg()` was the single place guaranteeing every interpolated identifier yields exactly one non-degenerate segment, and a future collection-level DELETE would silently become reachable by `<cmd> ''`. Keeping the throw for empty and giving the unset-workspace case its own explicit "no workspace selected" error would preserve both properties.
searchedFor: grep for a workspace-required guard in packages/cli/src (none found)

samples.summary: The short-lived code is still not bound to the flow that requested it — `POST /auth/cli/exchange` is unauthenticated bearer-of-the-code
samples.evidence: `createCode(user.id)` (auth.controller.ts:126, cli-auth.store.ts:62) stores only `{ userId, expiresAt }`; it is not tied to the `cliState` nonce, the port, or any CLI-held secret, and `cliExchange` (auth.controller.ts:152-168) requires no authentication. The code travels in the browser's URL bar to `127.0.0.1:<port>` and so lands in browser history (potentially cloud-synced) and in any local HTTP interception; whoever holds it within the 60-second TTL gets full access+refresh tokens for the user. The nonce added here protects the *listener*, not the *code*. Binding the code to the flow (store `cliState`/a CLI-held verifier with the code and require it on exchange) would make a leaked code useless to anyone but the CLI that started the flow.

verdict.reason: Verified in-repo. login.ts:40 mints the `state` nonce, login.ts:44-46 embeds it in the OAuth URL, login.ts:47 prints it to stderr, and login.ts:52 hands the full URL to `open()`, which spawns the platform opener with the URL as argv — readable by other local processes via /proc/<pid>/cmdline or ps, i.e. the exact attacker the comment at login.ts:33-39 claims to exclude. The nonce is the sole binding: stateMatches (login.ts:168-173, invoked login.ts:210) accepts any callback echoing that value, and POST /auth/cli/exchange (auth.controller.ts:152-168) requires only `{ code }` — no PKCE verifier or other per-flow secret. GitHubAuthGuard (github-auth.guard.ts:22-42) accepts attacker-supplied `port` and `cliState` with only a range check and CLI_STATE_PATTERN (:15), which a 43-char base64url nonce passes; CliAuthStore.createState (cli-auth.store.ts:27-43) stores them, and githubAuthCallback (auth.controller.ts:119-135) mints a code for the *authenticating attacker's* user and redirects it to the victim's loopback port with the stolen nonce. The victim's listener settles (login.ts:255-258) and saves the attacker's tokens as the session (login.ts:138-148) — the session-fixation/code-injection the change claims to close. The stored `csrf` value (cli-auth.store.ts:32) is never compared anywhere, so no guard elsewhere makes this unreachable. Docs repeat the unsupported claim (docs/design/rest-api.md:345-348, 374; docs/design/cli.md:198). In-lane (auth/crypto, session fixation), real, and not guarded — no refutation ground applies.

Anyone can therefore start a CLI flow aimed at an arbitrary loopback port with no binding whatsoever — e.g. a page the victim visits can navigate to `/auth/github?mode=cli&port=<guessed port>`. Today the new CLI rejects that (login.ts:210), so the exploit lands only against a CLI that has not been upgraded, or against any other consumer of this documented endpoint; but the server-side half of the mitigation is advisory. verdict.reason: The quoted code is present as described (github-auth.guard.ts:31-34 downgrades a missing/malformed cliState to undefined; auth.controller.ts:130-132 then emits no `state` on the loopback redirect), but the exploit chain is closed elsewhere and the proposed fix would close nothing. The CLI's loopback listener rejects fail-closed: stateMatches() returns false when `received === null` (login.ts:168-173) and the handler returns 400 without settling for any non-matching state (login.ts:206-214). It is the only in-repo consumer of the endpoint — grepping `mode=cli` across packages yields exactly one construction site, login.ts:45-46, which always mints a 32-byte nonce. Crucially, mandating cliState server-side blocks no attacker: an attacker who navigates the victim to /auth/github?mode=cli&port=N controls the whole query string and would just supply its own well-formed random nonce, which still fails stateMatches at login.ts:210 exactly as the empty case does. The redirect is otherwise constrained: host hard-coded 127.0.0.1, port range-checked in the guard (github-auth.guard.ts:30) and again on callback (auth.controller.ts:123-125), code/nonce URI-encoded, and codes single-use with 60s TTL (cli-auth.store.ts:62-77). The residual (a malicious local process binding the port) is unaffected by cliState either way. What remains is downgrade/compat hardening for non-validating legacy or third-party clients — minor, not a blocking security defect.

finding.summary: The CLI OAuth loopback callback has no `state`/CSRF binding, so any local process or visited web page can inject an attacker's authorization code and silently log the CLI into the attacker's account (pre-existing, out of diff)
finding.evidence: `startCallbackServer` (login.ts:168-182) resolves on the first `GET /callback?code=<anything>` it receives from 127.0.0.1, with no `state` parameter generated, no `state` echoed in the OAuth URL built at line 36 (`?mode=cli&port=${port}`), no Origin/Sec-Fetch check, and no binding between the code and this CLI invocation. The code is then exchanged at line 56 and the resulting tokens persisted with `saveSession` (line 138). Vector: while `wafflebase login` is waiting (30s window, line 237), a page the user is browsing — or any unprivileged local process — issues `fetch`/`img src` to `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=<attacker's code>` for candidate ports; the CLI exchanges the attacker's code and writes the attacker's `accessToken`/`refreshToken` and `activeWorkspace` into `~/.wafflebase/session.json`. Every subsequent `docs import` / `files upload` then writes the victim's data into the attacker's workspace. This is classic OAuth login-CSRF / session fixation. Out of the diff, but in the CLI auth path the diff's design doc explicitly discusses (`docs/design/cli.md`: 'The one command the flag does not hold back is `login`'). Fix: generate a random `state`, pass it in the OAuth URL, and reject a callback whose `state` does not match.

verdict.reason: The finding claims the CLI OAuth loopback callback has no state/CSRF binding, but the working tree contains a complete one. login.ts:40 mints a 32-byte nonce via randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'); line 41 passes it to startCallbackServer(state); lines 44-46 include it in the OAuth URL as &cliState=<nonce> (contradicting the reviewer's quoted URL); lines 206-214 reject any /callback whose state param does not match with 400 'State mismatch' WITHOUT settling the promise, so an injected code is never exchanged and the genuine callback can still arrive. Comparison at lines 168-173 is constant-time (timingSafeEqual with length pre-check). The echo leg exists server-side too: github-auth.guard.ts:26-40 validates/attaches cliState, github.strategy.ts:59-61 sets opts.state, cli-auth.store.ts:30-58 persists it, auth.controller.ts:130-131 echoes it on the loopback redirect as &state=. The described vector (browsed page or local process hitting 127.0.0.1:<port>/callback?code=...) is blocked at login.ts:210 because the attacker cannot know the nonce. Docs match (docs/design/rest-api.md:374, docs/design/cli.md:198). The reviewer appears to have read a stale version of login.ts.
